title: Clock & Voltage Sensitivity SKU Comparison — Lab Notes
content:
Summary
-------
These are lab notes for a focused investigation into how clock rate and voltage (power cap) settings interact with cloud GPU SKUs (A100 / H100 / L40S) and CUDA/driver combinations. Goal: surface brittle operating points that amplify tail latency or cause throughput regressions for our streaming decode workload (GPT-3.5-like decoder with kv-cache heavy prefill). This is intentionally a working note: experiment permutations are large and we prioritized conditions observed in customer incidents and our telemetry (spikes correlated with host clock/thermal transitions).

Key findings (high level)
-----------------------
- H100 (p5-like SKUs) shows the largest p99 sensitivity to aggressive power capping when CUDA context-switch rate is high (many small concurrent requests). p99 increased 2.2x at 70% power cap vs. nominal.
- A100 (p4/p4d-like) is most sensitive to suboptimal driver / CUDA combos: older drivers with CUDA 11.8 had measurable kernel launch serialization causing per-token p50 to increase by ~12%.
- L40S (GCP-style inference SKUs) exhibited more stable sustained throughput under reduced clocks, but suffered larger transient latency spikes during NVMe-backed KV spill events — likely due to PCIe ordering and DMA path differences.
- Mismatched driver/CUDA (driver newer than tested CUDA runtime) produced sporadic long-tail events on both A100 and H100; these events are absent when we pin the runtime to a driver/CUDA pair we validated.

Experimental setup
------------------
- Workload: streaming decode with prefill of 1k tokens per request, batch sizes: 1–8 concurrent requests. Mixed short and long tail sub-requests to emulate chat + longpass.
- Models: 6B dense decoder (baseline), 13B dense decoder for scale-checks.
- Instances & SKUs (lab inventory):
  - A100-80GB (p4d.24xlarge equivalent) — Ubuntu 22.04, driver 510.73.05, CUDA 11.8; also tested with driver 535.54 + CUDA 12.1.
  - H100-80GB (p5.24xlarge equivalent) — Ubuntu 22.04, driver 535.86, CUDA 12.1; also older driver 525.x tested.
  - L40S-48GB (gcp-l40s equivalent) — Ubuntu 22.04, driver 535.86, CUDA 12.1.
- Power/clock control: nvidia-smi and NVML where available; applied fixed clocks (nominal, -10%, -20%) and fixed power caps (100%, 85%, 70% of nominal).
- Software: serving-runtime branch: perf/clock-sensitivity (PR 2184), python client with deterministic request pacing to measure steady-state and tail behavior.
- Telemetry collected: per-token latency (p50/p90/p99), kernel launch times, PCIe counters where available, CPU steal/wait, NVML power and SM utilization, NVMe I/O latency and throughput when spill occurred.

Raw experimental observations
--------------------------
1) H100 — concurrent small requests (N=8) + 70% power cap
   - p50 token latency: +8% vs nominal (from 3.8ms -> 4.1ms)
   - p99 token latency: +120% vs nominal (from 28ms -> 62ms)
   - Kernel launch histogram: heavy right-tail; many micro-queuing events where kernels queued >500us before dispatch.
   - NVML: SM utilization unchanged, but average GPU clock oscillated with frequent NVS resets (~every 60–90s) correlated with a host daemon entering a thermal-safe mode.
   - Hypothesis: H100 firmware with aggressive power budget lets clocks oscillate under bursty multiplexing; power cap prevents recovery to nominal clocks, causing kernel wakeup delays.

2) A100 — mixed driver/CUDA setups
   - driver 510 + CUDA 11.8 (legacy): observed serialized kernel launches under heavy small-batch prefill traffic. p50 token latency increased 12% and tail p99 increased ~35%.
   - driver 535 + CUDA 12.1: baseline improved for steady-state throughput, but one-off long tails (~200–400ms) observed on ~0.03% of requests. eBPF traces show context preemption on CPU host scheduling path concurrent with NVML queries.
   - Hypothesis: older driver kernels serialize certain launch paths; newer drivers reduce base latency but expose host-side interactions (monitoring daemons) that can cause rare long tails.

3) L40S — NVMe spill coupling
   - Under heavy kv-cache pressure we triggered KV spill to NVMe on one config: p50 unchanged, p95/p99 had spikes to multiple seconds for a tiny fraction of requests.
   - PCIe counters show increased outstanding DMA transfers during spill. The L40S PCIe bridge has different scatter-gather characteristics compared to A100/H100 instances in our lab which likely increases completion jitter.
   - Recommendation: prefer in-memory KV allocations for L40S or tune spill thresholds; consider async spill pipeline to decouple NVMe sync latency from decode path.

Notable anomalies and reproduction notes
--------------------------------------
- Repro rate: the H100 power-cap p99 amplification reproducible ~95% across 12 repeated runs on same availability zone and host type; not reproducible on a different AZ (we suspect hypervisor power policy differences).
- One A100 host showed pathological behavior only when the host BIOS CPU C-state governor was set to 'powersave' — switching to 'performance' removed the long-tail events. Suggests host CPU power policies can interact with GPU kernel startup latency.
- Kernel-level driver logs (dmesg) on one H100 host show sporadic messages related to 'nvlink' link retraining coincident with tail spikes; link retrains were at times when the host performed live snapshot. Hard to reproduce intentionally.

Actionable recommendations for serving/runtime teams
--------------------------------------------------
1) Driver/CUDA matrix pinning: create a validated matrix for each SKU we serve and add pre-deployment checks in the private deploy installer to enforce recommended pairs. See linked PR 2184 for test harness.
2) Power policy defaults: for H100 SKUs targeted at latency-sensitive workloads, prefer 'no aggressive capping' defaults in our Dedicated/Private images; expose a control knob in Redwood Console for power caps with telemetry warnings when set.
3) KV spill tuning: make spill async by default for L40S customer images, and add a conservative threshold when running on L40S-type PCIe topologies.
4) Telemetry: add a tracer to record host CPU C-state transitions and NVML clock oscillation events alongside token-level latency. These were critical signals to correlate tail events.
5) Runbook: document a quick triage path for customers experiencing sudden p99 jumps: check driver/CUDA mismatch, verify host CPU gov, power cap, and NVMe queue depth.

Next experiments to prioritize
---------------------------
- AZ vs host-firmware correlation: reproduce H100 power-cap amplification across multiple cloud AZs and different hypervisor builds to determine if policy at hypervisor level is dominant.
- Controlled CPU C-states: systematically vary host CPU governor and C-states while running small-request high-concurrency workload on A100 and H100 to quantify impact on kernel startup.
- NVMe async spill prototype: implement async spill pipeline in perf branch and run L40S long-context workload to measure reduction in spike frequency.

Appendix: micro-observations and snippets
----------------------------------------
- Example NVML trace (trimmed):
  [2024-09-24T14:02:03Z] SM util 85%, clocks 1020/1410, power draw 210W
  [2024-09-24T14:02:03.620Z] clock drop -> 720/980 (host event)
  [2024-09-24T14:02:03.885Z] kernel queued 0.6ms -> dispatched
  [2024-09-24T14:02:03.892Z] decode token p99 spike = 83ms

- Quick checklist for reproducing H100 power-cap p99 amplification:
  1) Provision p5-like host in same AZ we used (request same instance id if possible).
  2) Use CUDA 12.1 + driver 535.86 baseline.
  3) Apply power cap to 70% via nvidia-smi.
  4) Run perf/clock-sensitivity harness with concurrency=8, prefill=1000.
  5) Collect NVML, dmesg, and eBPF scheduler traces.

Notes to self / unknowns
-----------------------
- We still don't have a conclusive causal chain for the H100 clock drops — could be hypervisor-level power thermal policies or an errata in the H100 microcode under multiplexed workloads. Need vendor engagement if we can reproduce on dedicated hardware under controlled datacenter conditions.
- Some customers reported similar tail patterns but with different exact numbers; I suspect orchestration layer (container/driver interaction) can amplify/amortize these effects.

References and links
--------------------
- GH PR perf/clock-sensitivity: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2184
- Jira: INFR-5001 (driver/cuda mismatch incidents)
- Confluence: GPU Driver Matrix Notes: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INFR/GPU+Driver+Matrix+Notes

--------------------

- Follow-ups: Maria will run AZ crosswalk. Liam will prototype async KV spill. Nina will add telemetry hooks for host CPU state and NVML clock transitions.
